To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
it is possible, to some extent, to predict whether a participant is a musician or not based on the thicknesses of the cortical regions of the brain.

it is possible, to some extent, to predict the group membership of a participant to a group of musicians or non musicians based on the thickness measurements of the cerebral cortex, and that the areas that contribute most to the classification were mostly in the left hemisphere, in the frontal, occipital, and parietal lobes, and that the distribution of the informative areas did not entirely overlap with earlier findings.

the thickness of the cortex can be measured at 148 regions of interest encompassing the whole cerebral cortex, and that this thickness can be used to predict with a significant accuracy whether a person is or is not a musician.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a method that can be used to predict whether a given individual is a musician or not, based on brain imaging data.
the question how the human brain is shaped by the environment.
the question whether it is possible to extract the information about an acquired skill such as playing an instrument, from the structure of the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

musical aptitude is reflected in the thickness of the cortex, and that it is possible for a machine to decode this information.

the brain is indeed plastic and that the structural plasticity can be decoded from the images.

decoding musical skills from magnetic resonance images can be used as a tool to study the neural basis of musical aptitude.
brain structure can be used to identify people with a particular skill.
the structure of the brain can be used to predict the acquisition of a skill.
